content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E012 (Christopher Myers) requests write access to Source Code.

Two notes:
- HR note: full_time Analyst, recommends write. Full-time employees allowed up to write.
- Security note: contractor, basic security training, recommends read. Contractors with basic training max out at read.

There's a discrepancy. HR says full-time, Security says contractor with basic training.

The access policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Source Code is owned by Engineer role. Christopher is an Analyst, not Engineer, so no admin either way.

If full-time: max is write, request write → grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read, request write → grant read.

The discrepancy matters. Who to trust? The security DB typically would be more authoritative for employment type? The notes say there's a discrepancy. Security DB shows contractor with basic security training.

Given the conflict, the safer/security-side decision is to grant the lower level: read. Since contractors with basic training max at read. The security note explicitly says the requested write must be reduced to read.

The policy says the maximum level an employee may have. If the employee is actually a contractor with basic training, max is read. Granting write would violate policy. Given conflicting info, we should err on the side of the more restrictive level to be safe.

So decision: read.

Evidence: Security DB shows contractor with basic security training; contractors with basic training max out at read; requested write exceeds max so grant max = read.

Let me submit.
